newsitem.title: UK: Dollar shy of 23-month peaks but still a good bet.
newsitem.headline: Dollar shy of 23-month peaks but still a good bet.

text.p: The dollar was just below 23-month peaks touched earlier on Tuesday against Europe's heavyweight currencies, but Germany's shaky economic recovery and Europe's progress towards monetary union will keep the dollar a favourite with investors, traders and analysts said on Tuesday.

"The general trend of the dollar continuing to strengthen is in place...But we are going to have some further hiccups on the road to monetary union and at those times we may see the deutschemark strengthen," said David Brickman, European analyst at Yamaichi International.

The dollar shot to 23-month highs against the mark, French franc and Swiss franc in overnight dealings after comments by German and U.S. officials on the dollar's status as a reserve currency before European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
But profit-taking later knocked the dollar off its 23-month peaks. At 1255 GMT, dollar/mark was at 1.5629 marks after powering to 1.5735, but remained up from 1.5445 marks in late Europe on Monday.
Traders said there had been hefty buying of dollars for French francs on Tuesday, and analysts said much of the dollar's gains in Europe had been led by French-franc weakness.
"This is mainly a function of what has happened within Europe, particularly given the amount of pressure for a French devaluation, which is clearly not on the cards," said Yamaichi's Brickman.
"For France to devalue now would actually put the whole EMU process into question," he added.

Comments by Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing and New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough on the dollar becoming more important in the run-up to EMU and Issing forecasting a possible shift from marks into dollars also provided a spark, said analysts.

"There are strong reasons why the deutschemark will suffer and the dollar will benefit ahead of monetary union. I see the dollar easily heading to 1.70 against the deutschemark," said DKB International Chief Economist Gerard Lyons.
Analysts said the possibility of a bigger role for the dollar as a reserve currency as an alternative to the mark is being discussed now because the Germans are worried about their economy.
Pan-German October industrial output, for instance, fell 1.8 percent month-on-month in November, its second consecutive month of weakness, and was much weaker than expected.

"In Germany, we are looking at what can be termed a bumpy recovery at best," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "The economic outlook should keep the mark soft against the dollar and its European crosses."
"The Germans are clearly worried about their domestic economy...The Bundesbank wants a weaker deutschemark," said DKB's Lyons.
Some dealers had also been speculating about a further cut in German interest rates. The Bundesbank eased the securities repurchase rate to 3.0 percent in August.
"I think the Germans will cut official rates. I think they will first cut the repo rate and then, they will cut the discount rate," said Lyons.
The Bundesbank on Tuesday declined to comment directly on the market's speculation about rate cuts in Germany.

But in response to a Reuter query on rates, chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber said the central bank had no direct comment on the talk, but added "I would draw your attention to recent comments by Mr Tietmeyer in Spiegel magazine, when he observed - I see no short-term reason for another interest rate change."
